title: Exercise
objective: After this level you can explain what exercise does for the heart, the muscles and the brain.
summary: WHO's 2020 guidelines: an average of 60 active minutes a day for ages 5 to 17, 150 to 300 a week for adults. Activity builds heart, lung, muscle and bone fitness and helps the brain.

cards.headline: About 4 in 5 teenagers worldwide don't move as much as the WHO recommends.
cards.body: A WHO-led study pooled surveys of 1.6 million students aged 11 to 17 and found 81 percent weren't active enough. So how much movement does the WHO actually suggest, and what does it do for you?

items.label: Ages 5 to 17
points: An average of 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity, mostly aerobic
Vigorous activity and muscle- and bone-strengthening on at least 3 days a week

items.label: Adults 18 to 64
points: 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate activity, or 75 to 150 of vigorous
Muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days a week

cards.headline: The talk test
cards.body: How hard is 'moderate'? The CDC has a shortcut: during moderate activity you can talk, but not sing. At vigorous intensity you can't say more than a few words without pausing for breath. And the WHO counts it all: walking, cycling, sports, active play, even getting around town. Its headline message is that any amount of activity is better than none. No gym membership required.

cards.headline: What it does for heart, muscles and brain
cards.body: The WHO lists the payoffs. For children and teens: fitter heart, lungs and muscles, better heart and metabolic health, stronger bones, and better thinking and mental health. For adults: lower risk of heart disease, high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes, better sleep, and fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression. The CDC adds that some brain benefits show up right after a single session. Your brain gets paid on the day.

cards.headline: Exercise: explained
learned: WHO 2020: ages 5 to 17 average 60 minutes a day
Adults: 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week
Talk test: moderate means talk but not sing
Benefits for heart, lungs, muscles, bones and brain

questions.prompt: Under WHO's 2020 activity guidelines, how much moderate-to-vigorous activity is recommended for young people aged 5 to 17?

options.label: An average of 60 minutes a day
150 minutes every single day
options.rationale: That's the adult weekly minimum, not a daily one.

options.label: Only on weekends, for 3 hours
options.rationale: The guideline is a daily average.

questions.explanation: WHO recommends ages 5 to 17 average 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous, mostly aerobic activity.

questions.prompt: You're cycling to school and can chat with a friend, but singing would be impossible. By the CDC's talk test, what intensity is that?

options.label: Vigorous
options.rationale: At vigorous intensity you can only manage a few words.

questions.explanation: Moderate activity lets you talk but not sing; vigorous activity leaves you pausing for breath after a few words.

questions.prompt: Vigorous exercise leaves you pausing for breath. Using Level 1's staircase, which two systems team up to get that extra oxygen to your muscles?

options.label: Skeletal and urinary
options.rationale: Bones hold you up; the urinary system filters blood.

options.label: Digestive and lymphatic
options.rationale: They handle food and fluid return.

questions.explanation: The respiratory system brings oxygen into the blood and the cardiovascular system carries it to working muscles.
